title: How To Handle A Bully Principal
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to reader mail about difficult administrators, Linsin argues that the single best defense against a bullying principal is simply never giving them a reason to target you. His guidelines include mastering classroom management so behavior issues never land on the principal's desk, refusing to flatter or ingratiate yourself with the boss, staying out of staff-lounge politics and gossip, and being first to turn in required paperwork, neatly done. He frames a principal's bad mood or curt tone as almost never about the teacher personally, and advises responding to any friction with calm, brief professionalism rather than anxiety or overexplaining. He closes with a personal anecdote about being snapped at over a broken cabinet, illustrating that competent, unbothered follow-through — not appeasement — is what earns a principal's lasting respect and leaves you alone.
points: Master classroom management so behavior issues rarely require principal involvement — the top source of administrator frustration.
Never try to ingratiate yourself, flatter the boss, or join their inner circle; competence earns respect more than sycophancy.
Stay out of staff-lounge politics, gossip, and campus opinionating, since word of it reliably reaches the principal.
Be first to submit required paperwork, neatly and completely done, to reduce the stress you add to an already pressured boss.
Treat a principal's curt tone or mood as rarely personal, and respond to any confrontation with calm, brief, unrattled professionalism.
quotes: They come in every size and shape, stripe and strata of education. And although their methods of torment may differ, the way to deal with them is the same: Don’t give them an opportunity.
Nothing gets under a principal’s skin more than having to deal with behavior issues. They have enough to worry about.
Be a pillar of competency and hang on tight to your self-worth. It’s the grovelers and sycophants who take the brunt of a wrathful boss.
Again, when your principal can count on you, when you don’t add stress to their already stressful life, they become deeply grateful you’re a member of the staff.
When you act nervously and walk on eggshells and worry over this and that you make the principal suspicious that perhaps you don’t have your act together.
I did my job well so nothing she could have said would have mattered.
And even if it is, most of the time it’s avoidable. If currently find yourself in the crosshairs, then follow the guidelines above. Slowly but surely, in a few weeks, they’ll forget about you.
